newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIAN PRESIDENT TO EXPLAIN PYRAMID SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIAN PRESIDENT TO EXPLAIN PYRAMID SCANDAL.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha plans to go to the angry town of Lushnje on Tuesday to explain his handling of a pyramid investment scandal which has sparked a month of protests and riots.
Officials said Berisha would travel to Lushnje, 85 km (53 miles) south of Tirana, in the afternoon to address a meeting of selected supporters of the ruling right-wing Democrats.
It will be the second time in four days that Berisha has tried to win support in the face of anti-government protests across the Balkan country.
On Saturday Berisha admitted that he had made mistakes in handling the pyramid scandal, in which thousands of Albanians lost money when five fraudulent schemes collapsed in January.
Berisha said that the investors themselves were ultimately responsible but admitted the government should have regulated the companies and warned investors sooner of their dangers.

He had tough words for Lushnje protesters who manhandled Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu, beating him badly when he arrived at a football stadium last month to discuss the scandal with beggared investors.

Berisha will try to avoid such a confrontation by limiting the size of his audience and making admission by invitation only. He is expected to address the group and take written questions from the floor.
In the southern port of Vlore, thousands of Albanians are expected to protest for a 14th day on Tuesday to demand the government pay compensation and then resign.
Berisha has said there will be no bailout with state funds, although the government has announced measures to take care of people who sold homes and apartments to invest more money.
About 5,000 people marched in Vlore on Monday, whistling, clapping and calling for Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi and his government to resign.
In a new twist, they sang regional songs but changed the words to ridicule ministers and accuse the government of taking their money.
Vlore students threatened to go on a hunger strike if the protesters' demands for compensation were not met.
"If by February 20 the people's demands are not met, the student leaders of Vlore university will go on hunger strike," they said in a petition.

"February 20 toppled dictatorships," they said, referring to the day in 1991 when protesters in Tirana tore down the statue of communist dictator Enver Hoxha, who ruled with an iron fist for 40 years.

Protests and riots have swept Albania for a month since the popular get-rich-quick investment schemes collapsed, posing the most serious challenge to the pro-market government since it came to power in 1992.
Vehbi Alimucaj, head of the biggest investment holding firm, Vefa, said angry investors should "roll up their sleeves and get back to work" instead of protesting and burning down buildings.
Vefa, a household name in Albania, froze the deposits of its 80,000 investors after the fraudulent pyramid schemes went bust last month and caused a panic.
Alimucaj told Reuters in an interview that his investors had nothing to fear and would get back their deposits in three or four months after a climate of insecurity had passed.
"We are prepared and proceeding with a definite timetable for paying this capital," he said. Meanwhile, Vefa had cash and was making interest payments to 2,000 to 3,000 people a day.
